To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the recurrence rate of pretransplant neoplasms is 20%, the recurrence rate of posttransplant neoplastic diseases is 30%, and that 50% of the recurrences of pretransplant cancers occur within 2 years following transplantation.

the risk of recurrence is highest for cancers treated within 2-5 year of transplantation, that the risk is lowest for neoplasms treated more than 10 years before transplantation, that a 2 year waiting period is desirable for the majority of neoplasms, that a 5 year period is desirable for lymphoma and for major carcinomas, and that no waiting period is necessary when the malignancy is small and has an excellent prognosis.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evaluation of transplant candidates with a prior history of cancer.
the evaluation and management of transplant candidates with a history of cancer.

the following: 1) The role of immunological mechanisms in the pathogenesis of human cancers; 2) The role of the immune system in the prevention and control of cancer; 3) The role of transplantation and immunosuppression in the development of human cancers.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

renal transplantation should not be performed in patients who have a history of cancer unless the cancer has been completely cured for at least two years, and the stage of the cancer does not have a high probability of recurrence or metastasis.

the risk for recurrence of a malignancy in a patient with renal failure, treated by renal transplantation, is dependent on the type of neoplasm, the time interval between treatment and transplantation, and the immunosuppressive regimen.
renal transplantation is not indicated for candidates who have had a malignancy, unless the disease is controlled and has been free from evidence of recurrence for 2 years.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

patients with a history of cancer should be considered for transplantation if they are free of disease for at least two years, if they are free from disease for at least five years and the cancer is of low grade, or if the cancer is of such a type that it is unlikely to recur.
the risk of tumor recurrence in renal transplant recipients is high, particularly among patients with a history of nonmelanoma cancers.

renal transplantation is not recommended for patients with active malignancies, and that a waiting period of two years after treatment of a malignancy is desirable for patients who are candidates for renal transplantation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the recurrence rate of treated neoplasms is high in renal transplant recipients, and the risk is highest within the first two years after transplantation.
the risk of recurrence of a preexisting malignancy in a patient with end-stage renal disease is not a contraindication for transplantation.
the risk of recurrence in patients with a history of cancer and who are undergoing transplantation is very high.
